papers.title: Limitations of nonreversible lifts for subgeometric diffusions
papers.abstract: We study the effect of lifting on continuous-time Markov processes with potentially subgeometric convergence rates. Using a series of weak Poincar\'e-type inequalities, we derive a bound on the maximum acceleration that can be obtained through lifting. We present several examples to explore the sharpness of our derived bound, where the resulting bound has the same square-root order as in the spectral gap setting. Our results provide a framework for understanding the potential and limitations of non-reversible lifting beyond geometric convergence.

papers.title: General coupling-based f-divergence diagnostics for Markov chain Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: A long-standing gap exists between the theoretical analysis of Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence, which is often based on statistical divergences, and the diagnostics used in practice. We introduce the first general convergence diagnostics for Markov chain Monte Carlo based on a broad class of f-divergence, allowing users to directly monitor, among others, the Kullback-Leibler and the chi-squared divergences as well as the total variation distance. Our approach rests on a coupling-based 'weight harmonization' scheme that produces direct, computable, and consistent importance weights for interacting Markov chains with respect to their target distribution. Beyond their use as convergence diagnostics, these weights give unbiased estimates of the Radon-Nikodym derivative between the un-normalized target and the distribution of the current iterate, a richer object than the convergence bounds alone, with natural applications to importance-weighted inference. We show how such weightings can provide asymptotic upper bounds to any f-divergence, prove that these bounds converge to zero as the chains approach stationarity, and demonstrate that, while more conservative than existing coupling-based total variation estimators, our method remains a practical and broadly applicable diagnostic tool.

papers.title: Does Increasing Government Spending on Tertiary Education Provide a Return on Investment? A Bayesian Causal Inference Analysis
papers.abstract: When a government increases public spending on tertiary (university) education, does it provide a positive fiscal return on investment once general economic growth is separated out? Cross-country data make this hard to answer because growing economies naturally collect more tax, international ratios divide per-student spending by GDP per person and student headcount, and cohorts take years to graduate. We assemble a five-year panel of 121 countries (1985-2024) and fit continuous-treatment Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests that model four tax changes jointly whilst adjusting for starting conditions, predicted funding, and follow-up economic growth. A +10 percentage-point (pp) increase in per-student university spending (% of GDP per person) shifts the tax mix toward direct income and profit taxation by +0.36 pp after 5 years (93% probability of a positive effect) and +0.71 pp after 10 years (96% probability). Overall tax-to-GDP takes a decade to respond as cohorts graduate: 10-year total non-resource tax rises by +0.24 pp of GDP (89% probability) and direct income tax by +0.12 pp (90% probability) per +10 pp of per-student spending, by +0.37 pp (100% probability) after five-year within-country funding increases, and by +0.22 pp in total tax (95% probability) and +0.15 pp in direct income tax (98% probability) per +25% increase in real PPP dollars per student. Comparing one entering cohort's degree cost against its 40-year career tax payments shows a typical three- to five-fold total tax return in high-income economies (EUR 2.37 billion in Ireland returning EUR 9.66 billion in total tax with a 77% probability of net profit and EUR 2.87 billion in direct income tax, or EUR 11.55 billion in the UK returning EUR 58.33 billion), whereas expanding the university budget without protecting spending per student yields no return.

papers.title: evgmrf: An R Package For Gaussian Markov Random Field Extreme Value Models
papers.abstract: We introduce \textsf{evgmrf}, an \textsf{R} package for fitting spatially varying extreme value models using Gaussian Markov random fields (GMRFs). The package supports the generalized extreme value distribution for block maxima, the generalized Pareto distribution for threshold exceedances, the Poisson--GPD point-process model, and the $r$-largest order-statistics model. Distributional parameters may vary over regular spatial grids or arbitrary regions that can be represented by a valid adjacency matrix, with optional fixed effects and covariate dependence. Spatial structure is represented through intrinsic conditional autoregressive, proper conditional autoregressive, and Besag--York--Molli\'{e} 2 models, which are extended with non-Gaussian random-effect distributions. Estimation uses penalized likelihood with smoothing or dependence hyper-parameters estimated using a Laplace approximation, exploiting sparse precision matrices for computational efficiency. The package provides methods for model summaries, spatial visualization, prediction on link and response scales, estimation of extreme quantiles, and uncertainty quantification in the form of approximate standard error estimates, or via simulations from parameter sampling distributions. Examples based on gridded and county-level precipitation data illustrate the use of the package for spatial modelling of environmental extremes. \textsf{evgmrf} provides a unified, accessible framework for extreme value analyses in which distributional parameters exhibit structured spatial variation.

papers.title: A fast and sound algorithm to simplify summations in interventional queries expressions
papers.abstract: Identification formulas returned by the ID algorithm often contain summations that can be removed. The procedure proposed in arxiv:1806.07082 (TK) removes them by combining factors of the formula into joint distributions, through the chain rule and through the insertion of factors for missing variables. We make two changes to this procedure: only the factors that involve the summed variable are combined, and every factor is written with a minimal conditioning set. These two changes determine the rest of the procedure, in which each search over a power set is replaced by a single test and the variables to insert are fixed in advance, and they remove summations that the TK procedure leaves in place. The resulting procedure is sound and, for minimal input terms, complete for each individual elimination with respect to joins and insertions.

papers.title: Node Localization by Multidimensional Scaling with Iterative Majorization
papers.abstract: Node localization aims to estimate the positions of nodes based on collected data from other nodes. Depending on the data characteristics, different procedures are utilized to estimate the locations. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive multidimensional scaling algorithm based on iterative majorization that comprises many of the different data characteristics to estimate node locations. The implicitly normalized loss function provides absolute distances and, given anchors, absolute node locations. The algorithm uses a new convergent coordinate descent procedure for the minimization of the majorization function, allowing for a natural treatment of anchors. Optimal transformations of the data seamlessly allows other data than Euclidean distances. Data from multiple sources, resulting in either asymmetric or three-way data, fit the same extensive framework.

papers.title: Efficiently Estimating Cycle Statistics on Graphs via Spanning Trees
papers.abstract: Simple cycles encode feedback and alternative routes in networks and are important for routing problems, the convergence of dynamical processes on networks, message passing and belief propagation, or even static network characterizations such as structural balance in signed networks. Being able to assess and sample from the cycle structure of a graph is thus of interest in many analysis contexts. However, due to the combinatorial growth of the cycle space with graph size, the computational cost for such sampling is high. Therefore, we here introduce a sampling framework that enables us to sample from the cycle structure without enumerating all cycles. Specifically, the method draws uniform spanning trees and collects the fundamental cycles created by their non-tree edges, such that each tree provides an informative subset of simple cycles. Because cycles are included with unequal probabilities and are dependent within each subset, we formulate an inclusion-probability-based Horvitz-Thompson estimator, which we average over random subsets, a procedure we call Monte Carlo Horvitz-Thompson. For this, we sample multiple Horvitz-Thompson estimators and introduce a method to further subsample the individual estimators for increased computational performance. For sampling cycles, the estimator is unbiased if exact cycle inclusion probabilities are known. To extend the method to larger networks, we derive an efficient mean-field approximation for the inclusion probabilities and characterize the graph regimes in which it remains accurate. Experiments on synthetic and real-world networks demonstrate the computational scaling and statistical performance of the framework. We then illustrate the utility of Monte Carlo Horvitz-Thompson estimation by estimating cycle counts and cycle-level frustration statistics in signed spin systems. An implementation is available in the py-raccoon package.
